endorsements.title: Adoption of AI in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts
endorsements.quote: From a clinical perspective, errors in documentation, such as attributing notes to the wrong person or ignoring critical details, pose risks.

evidence.title: Clinician Experiences with Ambient AI Scribe Technology in Singapore: A Qualitative Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported multilingual support limits of ambient AI scribe
evidence.effect: Clinicians identified limited multilingual functionality as a persistent barrier in Singapore's multilingual healthcare system; no quantitative rates reported.
evidence.quote: Persistent barriers included accuracy concerns, AI hallucinations, limited multilingual functionality, loss of documentation style, and uncertainties around compliance with the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA).

evidence.title: Performance of an Ambient Generative AI Documentation Tool in a Linguistically Diverse Clinical Setting
evidence.outcome: Ambient scribe performance in non-English encounters versus English encounters
evidence.effect: Non-English encounters were 21%–25% less likely than English encounters to achieve the same performance threshold.
evidence.quote: Non-English encounters were 21%–25% less likely than English encounters to achieve the same performance threshold.

evidence.title: Physician Perspectives on Ambient AI Scribes
evidence.outcome: Ambient scribe support for non-English speaking patients, per physician interviews
evidence.effect: Barriers to adoption included limited functionality with non-English speaking patients and lack of access for physicians without a specific device.
evidence.quote: Barriers to adoption included limited functionality with non-English speaking patients and lack of access for physicians without a specific device.

evidence.title: Ambient AI Documentation in Mixed-Language Encounters: A Heuristic Evaluation of Reenacted Mandarin–English and Spanish–English Clinical Conversations
evidence.outcome: Ambient scribe support for mixed-language (Mandarin–English, Spanish–English) encounters
evidence.effect: Low overall MER and reliable language switch detection, but frequent deletions at switch points in Mandarin–English transcripts and errors from phonetic similarity, automatic translation, and clinical terminology.
evidence.quote: The system generally detected language switches reliably, although deletions occurred frequently in Mandarin–English transcripts at switch points.

evidence.title: Large Language Models as a Consulting Hotline for Patients With Breast Cancer and Specialists in China: Cross-Sectional Questionnaire Study
evidence.outcome: LLM response accuracy and practicality in Chinese versus English queries
evidence.effect: Accuracy and practicality of ChatGPT-E were significantly higher than ChatGPT-C and EB for both questionnaires (all Ps<.001).
evidence.quote: Overall, for both the patient and expert questionnaire, the accuracy and practicality of responses from ChatGPT-E were significantly higher than those from ChatGPT-C and EB (all Ps<.001).

evidence.title: A hybrid large language model framework for structured data entry from code-switched persian clinical speech
evidence.outcome: ASR errors in Persian code-switched speech
evidence.effect: Whisper WER was 18.4% on standard Persian clinical speech and 28.7% in heavy code-switching segments.
evidence.quote: On the evaluation dataset, the Whisper model achieved a Word Error Rate (WER) of 18.4% on standard Persian clinical speech, increasing to 28.7% in segments exhibiting heavy code-switching.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether checking language support before adopting an ambient scribe improves documentation quality for patients who speak languages other than English. Six hazard studies suggest that scribe and speech tools perform worse in non-English and mixed-language encounters, which gives the recommendation a plausible rationale but no evidence of effect.

perspectives.view: No study evaluates pre-adoption language verification, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. Six studies document the hazard. The largest, with 54,160 encounters, found non-English encounters were 21% to 25% less likely to reach the performance threshold. The others are small qualitative or offline studies, and their findings agree in direction but are indirect for the practice.

In 24 reenacted Mandarin–English and Spanish–English visits, overall error rates were low, but Mandarin–English transcripts often dropped words at language switch points. Whisper's word error rate rose from 18.4% on standard Persian clinical speech to 28.7% in heavy code-switching. Such deletions may omit clinical details from notes, and no study shows whether pre-adoption checks catch them.

Clinicians in Singapore (n=28) and U.S. physicians (n=22) described limited multilingual function as a barrier during real deployments. These reports suggest that language gaps appear in daily workflow after rollout. Neither study examined whether vendor testing or local validation before purchase would have predicted the problem.

The 54,160-encounter study included safety-net and non-English populations and found lower performance for non-English encounters. A separate test found ChatGPT answers in English more accurate and practical than answers in Chinese (all Ps<.001), though that study concerns chatbot responses rather than scribes. No study reports results for low-literacy patients or tests whether verification narrows the gap.

Physicians reported limited function with non-English speaking patients as a barrier to use. This may mean these patients are less likely to benefit from scribe tools or more likely to receive notes with errors. No study asked patients with limited English proficiency about their experience or measured their trust in scribe-generated notes.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare scribe deployments with and without pre-adoption language validation and that measure note accuracy, omissions, and clinician editing time by patient language. These studies should include low-literacy patients and languages beyond Mandarin, Spanish, and Persian.
commentary.underserved_note: One real-deployment study included safety-net and non-English encounters, and three offline studies included non-English or mixed-language speech, but none tested the verification practice. Medicaid and low-literacy populations were not reported. The hazard evidence therefore covers some limited English proficiency groups, yet it cannot show whether verification protects them.
